newsitem.title: UK: Metals changes seen from regulator report Thursday.
newsitem.headline: Metals changes seen from regulator report Thursday.

text.p: Britain's top financial markets watchdog the Securities and Investments Board (SIB) is to release a report on Thursday expected to advise changes in London's opaque industrial metals market.
The report by the SIB was commissioned by the London Metal Exchange (LME) after the Sumitomo Corp scandal rocked financial markets in June this year.
"The report will come out on Thursday," a SIB spokeswoman told Reuters on Monday.
The SIB is expected to suggest changes in the 120-year-old LME, the world's centre for trading in industrial metals.

Confidence in the LME was eroded in June when Sumitomo fired its head copper trader Yasuo Hamanaka, triggering a crash in copper prices. The giant Japanese conglomerate says Hamanaka ran up losses of $2.6 billion in unauthorised copper trading.
Traders say changes are destined for the LME, which is accustomed to an old-world manner that relies more on gentlemanly handshakes than written regulations.
"It (the LME) had been changing for some years anyway. Sumitomo and the SIB will probably accelerate that process," one senior trader said last week.
The chairman of the LME Raj Bagri has said he would be ready to tighten regulations and said the LME needed greater transparency.
But he has stoutly defended the LME's role leading up to the Sumitomo scandal, saying that many of the deals were private ones between trading firms and not recorded on the exchange.
In making its review, the SIB consulted traders, consumers and producers, sending a 33-question document around the world.

The watchdog said in October after it had received initial replies to its questionnaire that users of the LME want more information, but they differ on whether the additional data should be in the public domain or just available to regulators.

Industry sources said the SIB may suggest that the LME require daily reporting of inventory movements, the revelation of ownership of those inventories in warehouses and more transparency in market positions.
Changes in LME membership may also be advised.
The New York Mercantile Exchange (NYMEX), which also trades copper, has proposed sweeping reforms of its rival which it said failed to provide proper controls leading up to the Sumitomo losses.
NYMEX said the LME should copy the New York exchange and institute a cash clearing system.
Presently, positions on the LME only become payable when the due date becomes prompt and so called "historic price carries" allow customers to roll forward expiring positions.
NYMEX says this allows players to mask the impact of any losses.
